purpose: Avapritinib is used to treat certain types of gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), which are cancers that grow in the digestive tract. It is also used for a rare bone marrow condition called advanced systemic mastocytosis. Your doctor prescribed it because your specific cancer or condition has certain gene changes that this medicine targets.
how_it_works: Your cancer cells have an abnormal protein caused by a gene mutation that tells them to grow out of control. Avapritinib works like a precision lock-and-key — it specifically blocks that abnormal protein, slowing or stopping cancer cell growth. Because it targets only the abnormal protein, it can be more precise than traditional chemotherapy.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or weak, nausea, swelling in your hands or feet, diarrhea, feeling dizzy, decreased appetite, vomiting, hair color changes, watery eyes, stomach pain, and changes in your memory or thinking (cognitive effects like forgetfulness or confusion).
warnings: This medicine can cause serious brain-related side effects including confusion, memory problems, speech difficulties, and in rare cases, bleeding in the brain — tell your doctor right away if you notice any thinking or mood changes. It can harm an unborn baby, so effective birth control is very important during treatment and for a period after stopping. Avoid driving or operating machinery if you feel dizzy or confused. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, as many drugs can interact with avapritinib.
typical_dosing: For GIST, the usual dose is 300 mg taken by mouth once daily on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating). For systemic mastocytosis, the usual dose is 200 mg once daily, also on an empty stomach. Always take it at the same time each day, and swallow the tablet whole — do not crush or chew it. If you miss a dose, skip it and take the next one at your regular time.
